brief.prompt: Raw material. The empirical Lorenz curve L(P) answers: of total mean latency, how much is contributed by requests faster than percentile P. Requests at or above p50 account for ~99% of mean latency; requests at or above p99 account for ~52%. Little's law makes that same fraction the share of system concurrency: in a threaded service, if 1-L(p)=k then 100k% of busy threads are occupied by requests that will finish above the pth percentile. Values of 1-L(0.99) above 0.5 or 0.75 are common. Constraints: tail alpha must exceed 1 or the mean is not estimable; measured percentiles are themselves estimates and uncertainty grows with the percentile. Write a design doc for a capacity and performance team on how to prioritise latency work against cost.

brief.prompt: Raw material. Two disputes. A service reports mean request time of 100ms; a user reports her mean wait is 1s. If the operator's mean is E[X], the customer-experienced mean is E_a[X] = E[X^2] / (2 E[X]) = 0.5 * (E[X] + Var(X)/E[X]). Timeout-and-retry can hide some service-time tail, but nothing hides recovery-time tail. Write a design doc for a platform org proposing how availability and recovery should be measured.

brief.prompt: Raw material. Paul E. McKenney published Stochastic Fairness Queuing in 1990. Baseline fairness queuing keeps a separate FCFS queue per conversation and services queues bit-by-bit round-robin; ill-behaved conversations that exceed their fair share get longer delays and higher packet loss than well-behaved ones. The same construction works for RPC traffic by keying on something else, such as authorized customer id, instead of a source-destination address pair. Cost of the baseline in a distributed system: O(customers) queues plus O(customers) work to round-robin across them. SFQ replaces per-conversation queues with a fixed set of queues and a simple hash mapping into them: O(1) queues, O(1) time. New problem: two conversations that collide keep colliding, so each persistently receives less than its share. Remedy: periodically perturb the hash function so colliders in one period are unlikely to collide in the next. A further variant combines SFQ with shuffle sharding and best-of-two: map each customer to a subset of queues (possibly just two), enqueue each request into the shortest queue in that customer's subset, and periodically perturb subsets. Properties: O(1) queues, O(1) enqueue, O(1) dequeue, strong noisy-neighbour isolation provided only a small portion of customers are noisy. Usable on a single host or across hosts for load balancing. Write a design doc proposing a request-queuing scheme for a multi-tenant RPC service.

brief.prompt: Raw material. Aurora DSQL's stated goal: a relational database that removes scale, reliability, durability, and multi-region fault tolerance from what an application builder has to think about. A database of first resort, simple to adopt at low scale, growing with the application without adding complexity. The operational-simplicity argument applies to human-built systems and is magnified for agent-built ones, because agents build well but are weak at long-horizon tasks such as database operations. The architecture is disaggregated: multiple independent services, each owning a small number of well-defined concerns. DSQL is not the first disaggregated OLTP database; Aurora and DynamoDB came earlier. The lessons carried over from operating those at scale: avoid large caches, which make failovers and read scaling awkward; offer strongly consistent scalable reads, which removes whole classes of hot-key and partition problems; push expensive operations such as scans down into storage, where they run next to local SSD. DSQL goes further than predecessors by fully disaggregating replication from transaction isolation and from storage. Multi-tenant packing reduces the peak-to-average load ratio on a physical machine at approximately the rate of sqrt(number of loads); cost scales with peak while revenue scales with average. The same packing argument appeared in the Firecracker paper. Write an architecture design doc for a team building a new disaggregated data service.

brief.prompt: Raw material. Framing for coding-agent capability, from an electrical-engineering analogy. Coding agents now build meaningful, correct software quickly and at very low cost, with super-human ability on some coding tasks. brief.prompt: Raw material. The feedback loop hypothesis: in the long term, coding agents will find tasks with effective feedback easy and tasks without effective feedback hard, and the availability of accurate feedback sets the limit on their capability. Current evidence. Good error messages keep agents unstuck. Rust steers agents toward correct code by signalling some kinds of incorrectness explicitly and immediately. Agents do well on performance work where good benchmarks exist. Property-based testing is unusually valuable. Agents do poorly on architecture, where feedback is of the know-it-when-I-see-it kind, and on concurrent programs, where feedback arrives as silent data corruption at runtime. Two comparison problems: building a delightful, ergonomic photo-editing website, and building a correct high-performance database storage engine at the scale of RocksDB or InnoDB, not Aurora DSQL or PostgreSQL. For open-loop models the website is easier and gets closer to success in a single shot. The hypothesis inverts this over the long run: the website's loop needs a human, and humans are slow, squishy, inconsistent feedback providers, while the storage engine has a simple specification covering API, safety properties, and liveness properties, so iteration needs no human. Implied tooling: Rust, Hydro, Verus at compile time; TLA+ and P at modelling time; Kiro's spec analyzer; testing tools, simulators, mocks. Write a design doc for engineering leadership on where to invest in agent tooling.
